title: Career guidance and pathway counselling under CBE
description: How Kenyan senior school principals can build a genuinely effective career guidance programme that helps students make informed pathway and post-school decisions under CBE.
body:
CBE places students at a significant decision point earlier than the old 8-4-4 system did — choosing between STEM, Social Sciences, and Arts and Sports Science pathways at the start of senior school. This makes genuine career guidance not a nice-to-have but a structural necessity, since a poorly informed pathway choice at Grade 10 can close doors that are difficult to reopen by Grade 12.

Guidance needs to start before pathway selection, not after

Many Kenyan schools treat career guidance as a Grade 12 activity focused on university applications. Under CBE, the more critical intervention point is earlier — helping students understand what each pathway leads to before they choose it, not after they have committed to three years of study in a direction that may not suit their interests or aptitudes.

Move beyond generic aptitude talk to real information

Career guidance that consists only of general encouragement — "follow your passion," "work hard" — does not give students what they actually need, which is concrete information: what subjects and grades specific careers require, what the job market realistically looks like in different fields, and what the pathway from a chosen subject combination to a career actually involves.

A practical resource: The National Industrial Training Authority (NITA) and various professional bodies publish career pathway guides that map subject combinations to career and training options. Schools that use these structured resources, rather than relying solely on staff general knowledge, give students more accurate guidance.

Individual guidance, not only group sessions

Group career talks are useful for broad information but cannot substitute for individual conversations that account for a specific student's interests, strengths, and circumstances. Schools with the capacity to offer even brief individual guidance sessions — 15 minutes per student during Term 2 or 3 of Grade 10 or 11 — report that students make more confident, better-informed pathway and subject decisions than those relying only on group sessions.

Engage parents in the guidance process

Parental expectations significantly influence student pathway and career decisions in the Kenyan context — sometimes helpfully, sometimes in ways that conflict with a student's genuine aptitude or interest. A guidance programme that includes parents — through a dedicated parent session on CBE pathways and career options — helps align family expectations with realistic, student-appropriate choices, reducing the tension that arises when a student's genuine interests differ from parental hopes.

Build relationships with tertiary institutions and employers

Schools that build ongoing relationships with local universities, TVET institutions, and employers — through career days, site visits, or guest speakers — give students exposure to real options that a classroom conversation cannot replicate. These relationships also often produce internship or attachment opportunities that benefit Grade 11 and 12 students directly.

Track outcomes to improve guidance over time

Few Kenyan schools systematically track what happens to their graduates — which pathways led to which outcomes, which guidance approaches correlated with successful transitions. A simple alumni tracking practice, even informal, gives a school genuine evidence about whether its career guidance approach is actually working, rather than relying on assumption.
